chapters.title: Chapter 5: Filing Your Return Step by Step

lessons.title: Computing Tax Payable: Self-Assessment Tax, Interest and Refunds

body.text: The balance on your return is rarely the whole bill. If you owed more than ₹10,000 beyond TDS, the law expected you to pay it during the year, and it charges 1% a month for every month you did not.

children.text: The portal computes all of this for you in the Total Tax Liability section. But if you do not understand where the numbers come from, you cannot tell whether they are right, and you cannot avoid them next year. This lesson rebuilds the portal's calculation by hand, for one taxpayer who owes tax and one who is due a refund.

body.caption: A positive balance is paid as self-assessment tax before filing. A negative balance is your refund.

children.text: Step 1: Work Out the Tax Still Due

Rohan, 35, is a product lead in Bengaluru on a salary of ₹20,00,000, in the new regime. He also rents out a flat in Whitefield for ₹40,000 a month, with no loan and no municipal tax paid by him in the year. His employer deducted TDS on salary. His tenant, paying less than ₹50,000 a month, deducted none. He paid no advance tax.

cells: Add: house property income (₹4,80,000 rent less 30%)
Less: TDS on salary, computed by employer on ₹19,25,000
Assessed tax still due, before interest

children.text: Step 2: Were You Supposed to Pay Advance Tax?

markDefs.definition: Tax paid in instalments during the financial year on estimated income, instead of in one go after the year ends. Required when tax payable after TDS and TCS is ₹10,000 or more.

children.text: If your tax for the year, after TDS and TCS, is ₹10,000 or more, you must pay

in four instalments during the year. Salaried people usually never think about it because TDS covers their tax. The moment you have rent, interest, capital gains or freelance income that nobody deducts tax on, the obligation can quietly appear. Rohan's ₹83,460 is well above ₹10,000, so he was required to pay advance tax on the dates below.

stats.label: By 15 June 2025
stats.context: Of tax due for the year

body.label: Exempt From Advance Tax
body.value: Resident senior citizens with no business income
body.context: A resident aged 60 or above at any time during the year, with no income from business or profession, need not pay advance tax, so no interest for missed instalments applies. Late filing interest still does.

body.caption: Interest for Late Filing and Late Payment

cells: Return filed after the due date
Tax still unpaid on the due date
From the day after the due date to the date of filing
Advance tax paid is less than 90% of assessed tax
Assessed tax minus advance tax paid
From 1 April after the year ends to the date of payment
Any instalment paid late or short
3 months each for the June, September and December instalments; 1 month for March

body.text: Three rules make the numbers work. The rate is 1% a month, simple interest. Any part of a month counts as a full month. And the amount on which interest is calculated is rounded down to the nearest ₹100. There is also some tolerance: under the interest for missed instalments, no interest is charged on the first instalment if you paid at least 12% by 15 June, or on the second if you paid at least 36% by 15 September.

body.title: Compute Rohan's Interest for Not Paying Advance Tax
body.prompt: Rohan paid none of his ₹83,460 of assessed tax as advance tax, so the interest for advance tax default applies. He pays self-assessment tax on 25 July 2026. Remember: 1% a month, part months count in full, and the amount is rounded down to the nearest ₹100. How much interest applies?
body.explanation: Advance tax paid is nil, which is less than 90% of assessed tax, so interest applies. The period runs from 1 April 2026 to 25 July 2026: April, May and June are full months and July is a part month, so 4 months. The amount rounded down is ₹83,400. Interest is ₹83,400 × 1% × 4 = ₹3,336.

body.caption: Rohan's Self-Assessment Tax Challan, Paid 25 July 2026

children.text: Self-assessment tax, under Section 140A of the Income-tax Act, 1961, must cover the tax and the interest before you file. Now see what happens if Rohan puts it off and files on 20 September 2026 instead, paying the same day. Late filing interest runs for August and part of September, the advance tax interest period stretches to six months, and a ₹5,000 late fee under Section 428 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 234F of the 1961 Act) is added.

body.title: Rohan's Interest and Fees: Filing on 25 July vs 20 September 2026 (₹)
The Cost of Waiting
body.prompt: Using the chart, how much more does Rohan pay in interest and fees by filing and paying on 20 September 2026 instead of 25 July 2026?
body.explanation: On 25 July: ₹3,336 + ₹4,209 = ₹7,545. On 20 September: late filing interest of ₹83,400 × 1% × 2 months = ₹1,668, advance tax default interest of ₹83,400 × 1% × 6 months = ₹5,004, the same ₹4,209 for missed instalments, and the ₹5,000 late fee, totalling ₹15,881. The difference is ₹8,336, for waiting under two months.

body.title: The Advance Tax Threshold
body.textWithBlank: Interest for advance tax default applies when the advance tax you paid during the year is less than ___% of your assessed tax.
body.explanation: If you paid at least 90% of your assessed tax as advance tax by 31 March, there is no interest for advance tax default, although interest for individual late or short instalments can still apply.

body.text: Capital gains and dividends get relief. If a gain or dividend arises after an instalment date, you are not expected to have paid tax on it in the earlier instalments, as long as you pay it in the remaining instalments, or by 15 March if it arises late in the year. So a gain booked in January only needs to be covered by the March instalment. Rent and salary do not get this relief, because they are regular income you can foresee.

body.title: Avoiding Rohan's Interest Next Year
body.question: Rohan will earn the same rent in FY 2026-27. Which step avoids most of the interest he paid this year?
options: Filing his return on 1 April 2027, as soon as the year ends
Declaring the rental income to his employer so TDS covers it, or paying advance tax on schedule
body.explanation: The interest arises because tax on the rent was not paid during the year. Employees can give their employer details of other income so that salary TDS is increased to cover it, or pay advance tax themselves by each instalment date. Filing early or paying by 31 July only stops the advance tax default interest from growing further; it does not undo interest for missed instalments. Switching regimes does nothing about timing.

children.text: The Other Side: When the Balance Is a Refund

Priya, a school teacher in Jaipur, has total tax of ₹48,000 for FY 2025-26 after cess. TDS on her salary and FDs came to ₹55,500. Her balance is negative: a refund of ₹7,500. If she files by the due date, the department adds interest at 0.5% a month from 1 April 2026 under Section 437 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 244A of the 1961 Act). No interest is paid if the refund is less than 10% of the tax determined, but Priya's refund is about 15.6% of ₹48,000, so she qualifies.

columns.label: When You Owe Tax
points: Pay self-assessment tax, including interest, before filing
Interest at 1% a month for missed advance tax and late filing
Unpaid tax at filing can make the return defective
Late filing adds a fee of up to ₹5,000

columns.label: When You Are Owed a Refund
points: File and e-verify; no payment needed
The department pays interest at 0.5% a month
Interest runs from 1 April only if you file by the due date
Refund goes to your pre-validated bank account after processing

body.title: The January Share Sale
body.scenario: Nikhil, a salaried engineer in Chennai, has all his salary tax covered by TDS. In January 2026 he sold shares held for eight months, making a short-term gain of ₹2,00,000. He did not pay any advance tax, and he pays the tax on the gain as self-assessment tax on 20 July 2026, before filing.
body.prompt: Work out the tax on the gain, whether interest applies, and how much. What should he have done instead?
body.modelAnswer: Tax on the short-term gain is 20% of ₹2,00,000 = ₹40,000, plus 4% cess of ₹1,600, so ₹41,600. That is above ₹10,000, so advance tax applied. Because the gain arose in January, after the June, September and December instalment dates, no interest applies to those three instalments; the full ₹41,600 was due by 15 March 2026. Interest for the missed March instalment is ₹41,600 × 1% × 1 month = ₹416. He also paid less than 90% of assessed tax as advance tax, so interest for advance tax default runs from 1 April to 20 July 2026, which is 4 months: ₹41,600 × 1% × 4 = ₹1,664. Total interest is ₹2,080, and his self-assessment tax challan should be ₹41,600 + ₹2,080 = ₹43,680. Had he paid ₹41,600 as advance tax by 15 March 2026, he would have paid no interest at all.

body.title: Before You Accept the Portal's Numbers
steps: Rework total tax: slab tax, rebate if any, special rate tax on gains, and cess
Subtract every TDS, TCS, advance tax and self-assessment tax credit
If the balance is ₹10,000 or more and you are not an exempt senior citizen, expect interest for advance tax default and missed instalments
Check whether any capital gain or dividend arose late in the year, which reduces instalment interest
Add late filing interest and the late fee if you are past the due date
Pay the tax and all interest in one self-assessment challan before filing
Next year, pay advance tax on non-salary income by the instalment dates, or ask your employer to include it in TDS

points: The balance on your return is tax on total income less rebate plus cess, minus TDS, TCS and advance tax, plus interest and any late fee

Advance tax is due in instalments of 15%, 45%, 75% and 100% by 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March when tax after TDS is ₹10,000 or more; resident seniors without business income are exempt
Section 424 (234B) charges 1% a month from 1 April if less than 90% of assessed tax was paid in advance; Section 425 (234C) charges 1% a month on each instalment shortfall
Section 423 (234A) adds 1% a month from the day after the due date when filing late with tax unpaid, and Section 428 (234F) adds a late fee
Part months count as full months, the amount is rounded down to ₹100, and capital gains or dividends arising later in the year only need to be covered by the remaining instalments
Refunds earn 0.5% a month under Section 437 (244A), from 1 April if filed by the due date, provided the refund is at least 10% of the tax determined

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Interest computations are simplified illustrations; the portal and the department apply detailed rules on rounding, the order in which payments are adjusted, and exceptions. Rates, thresholds and section numbers reflect FY 2025-26 and the Income-tax Act, 2025 at the time of writing. Rely on the portal's computation or a qualified tax professional for your return.
